modelNote:
Create a clean, professional portrait infographic for university students summarising the paper: “Decreasing students’ stress through time management training: an intervention study” by Alexander Häfner, Armin Stock & Verena Oberst, Eur J Psychol Educ (2015) 30:81–94. DOI 10.1007/s10212-014-0229-2. Published online 6 September 2014.

STRICT SOURCE RULES: Use only the paper content below. Do not add any outside facts, examples, or numbers. Keep claims hedged exactly. Use the paper’s names: perceived stress was measured with “tension”; “demands” means perceived, self-reported demands. Do not calculate new values. Every number must exactly match the paper.

STYLE: Portrait/tall infographic, clear hierarchy, title at top. Clean academic design, readable, modern, white background with blue/teal accents and small orange highlight. Use icons, simple charts, timeline, and mini line charts. Prefer fewer larger text blocks. Spell every word correctly.

TITLE SECTION:
Title: “Time management training and student stress”
Subtitle: “Infographic summary of Häfner, Stock & Oberst (2015)”

SECTION 1 — PURPOSE (use target icon):
Heading: “Research question”
Text: “Can time management training increase perceived control of time and reduce perceived stress (tension) in undergraduate students?”
Hypotheses: “Perceived control of time ↑”; “Perceived stress (tension) ↓”; “Demands unchanged”

SECTION 2 — SAMPLE + DESIGN (use student/person icons and a 3-step timeline):
Heading: “Sample and design”
Text bullets:
“48 local undergraduate students began the study”
“23 completed all questionnaires and were used in the main analyses”
“Mean age = 23.30 years (SD = 2.80)”
“52% female”
“Single trained group; non-equivalent dependent variable design”
Timeline: “Time 1: directly before training” → “Time 2: 2 weeks after” → “Time 3: 4 weeks after”
Small note: “Demands was the control variable expected not to change.”

SECTION 3 — TRAINING CONTENT (use five linked cards/icons):
Heading: “4 h time management training”
Five cards:
1. “Prioritizing”
2. “Concrete, challenging and proximal goals”
3. “Strategy development and obstacles”
4. “Daily planning and implementation intentions”
5. “Monitoring task completion”
Include text: “Held in the middle of the semester in groups of about ten students.”

SECTION 4 — KEY MEASURES (small scale icons):
Heading: “What was measured”
Three compact cards:
“Time management behaviour: 18 items, 1 = nearly never to 5 = nearly always”
“Perceived control of time: 10 items, 1 = nearly never to 5 = nearly always”
“Perceived stress (tension): 5 items, 1 = never to 5 = always”
“Demands: 5 items, 1 = never to 5 = always”

SECTION 5 — RESULTS (main visual section with line charts; use exact means):
Heading: “Key results”
Create three small line charts with x-axis labels “Before”, “2 weeks”, “4 weeks”. Do not add derived changes.
Chart 1 title: “Perceived stress (tension)”
Values labelled exactly: 3.30, 2.96, 3.03
Annotation: “Significantly less stress at 2 weeks and 4 weeks vs. before training.”
Stats text: “2 weeks: F(1,22)=8.22, partial η²=0.27, p<0.01” and “4 weeks: F(1,22)=5.75, partial η²=0.21, p=0.03”
Chart 2 title: “Perceived control of time”
Values labelled exactly: 2.75, 2.89, 3.05
Annotation: “2 weeks: tendency in the expected direction; 4 weeks: significant increase.”
Stats text: “2 weeks: F(1,22)=3.38, partial η²=0.13, p=0.08” and “4 weeks: F(1,22)=11.62, partial η²=0.35, p<0.01”
Chart 3 title: “Demands”
Values labelled exactly: 3.59, 3.35, 3.46
Annotation: “No significant changes.”
Stats text: “2 weeks: t(22)=1.68, p=0.107” and “4 weeks: t(22)=1.19, p=0.251”
Also include small result card: “Time management behaviour increased significantly from before training to 4 weeks after: t(22)=2.67, p<0.01 (one-tailed), ε′=0.79. The 2-week increase was nearly significant: t(22)=1.62, p=0.060 (one-tailed), ε′=0.48.”

SECTION 6 — PRIOR EXPERIENCE (small comparison note, no extra chart unless simple):
Heading: “Who seemed to benefit more?”
Text: “Students with no or little time-management experience seemed to profit more from training than students with moderate or some experience, especially with respect to perceived stress.”
Include exact effect sizes only as text:
“At 4 weeks, no/little experience: ε′=0.78 for perceived control of time; ε′=0.64 for perceived stress.”
“Moderate/some experience: ε′=0.34 for perceived control of time; ε′=0.13 for perceived stress.”

SECTION 7 — AUTHORS’ INTERPRETATION + LIMITATION (use lightbulb and caution icons):
Heading: “What the authors conclude”
Text: “The pattern of changes in the intended variables, with no change in demands, supports the conclusion that the training led to decreased perceived stress and increased perceived control of time.”
Heading: “Main limitation”
Text: “Small sample size: the authors describe the study as preliminary and call for larger samples and more intervention studies.”
Additional limitation line: “An experimental design with a control group, especially pseudo-training groups, would be a methodological improvement.”

BOTTOM TAKEAWAY (large highlighted box):
Heading: “Takeaway”
Text: “A 4 h time management training might be beneficial for undergraduate students’ well-being, but more studies with larger samples are necessary for more robust conclusions.”

Ensure the final image is a single portrait infographic with all text readable and not overcrowded.
